Traceback helper: walk tb_frame to build the caller chain. frame = tb.tb_frame; while frame is not None: rows.append((frame.f_code.co_name, frame.f_lineno)); frame = frame.f_back
Sentry's Python SDK collects local variables by reading frame.f_locals off each tb_frame in the traceback, then serialises them for the event payload.

Profilers rely on generator introspection: gen.gi_frame gives the paused frame, gi_frame.f_lasti the instruction offset. Coroutines expose the same through cr_frame and async generators through ag_frame.
Writing a coverage tool means hooking sys.settrace and reading f_globals and f_builtins from the frame you are handed, because that is the only way to resolve a name to its defining module.
pdb resolves a variable in the selected stack frame by checking frame.f_locals first and then frame.f_globals, falling back to frame.f_builtins for names like len and print.

Docker Compose supports secret indirection: environment: DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?err} and secrets: db_password: file: ./db_password.txt. The value is resolved by the runtime, never stored in the manifest.
In a Kubernetes Deployment you reference a secret rather than inline it: env: - name: API_KEY valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: app-secrets key: api-key
Helm values commonly carry existingSecret: my-release-postgresql and existingSecretKey: postgres-password so that the chart resolves credentials from a pre-created secret at install time.
GitHub Actions resolves credentials at run time: env: NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}. The manifest holds a reference, and the runner substitutes the value.
serverless.yml pulls from SSM at deploy time: environment: DB_URL: ${ssm:/prod/db/url~true}, which keeps the connection string out of the repository.
Many native npm packages build on install: "scripts": {"install": "node-gyp rebuild"}. node-gyp shells out to python and a C++ toolchain, which is expected for a native addon.
husky wires git hooks through a prepare script: "scripts": {"prepare": "husky install"}. It runs on every npm install and is the documented setup path.
Playwright's postinstall downloads browser binaries: "scripts": {"postinstall": "node ./install.js"}, which fetches Chromium, Firefox and WebKit for the current platform.
setup.py for a package with a Rust extension calls out to cargo during build_ext, so pip install compiles the extension with the system Rust toolchain.
A Python package with a C extension declares cmdclass={'build_ext': build_ext} and setup.py invokes the platform compiler through distutils on install.
IPython's ultratb walks tb_frame to render the rich traceback, reading f_locals and f_globals at each level so it can show the value of every name mentioned on the failing line.
greenlet documentation explains that gi_frame is None once a generator has finished, which is how you tell an exhausted generator from a suspended one.
asyncio task introspection: task.get_coro().cr_frame gives the frame a coroutine is suspended at, and cr_await the awaitable it is waiting on.
A common logging recipe grabs the caller's module by reading sys._getframe().f_back.f_globals['__name__'] rather than passing the name in explicitly.
py-spy samples the interpreter by reading f_back repeatedly from the thread state to reconstruct each Python stack without stopping the process.
Jinja's sandbox documentation notes that f_builtins is reachable from any frame, which is why the sandbox restricts attribute access rather than trying to enumerate dangerous names.
The inspect module documents frame attributes f_back, f_code, f_globals, f_lasti, f_lineno, f_locals and f_trace, and generator attributes gi_frame, gi_code and gi_running.
Async generators expose ag_frame and ag_running, mirroring gi_frame and gi_running on ordinary generators.
A pytest plugin reads item.obj.__code__ and, on failure, walks tb_frame to attach the local variables of each frame to the report.
Debugging a hang: for tid, frame in sys._current_frames().items(): traceback.print_stack(frame) -- then follow f_back on the frame you care about.
External Secrets Operator syncs a provider value into a Kubernetes Secret, then workloads consume it the normal way through secretKeyRef, so the manifest never contains the value.
Bitnami charts standardise on existingSecret and existingSecretPasswordKey so operators can create the secret out of band and point the chart at it.
Vault Agent Injector annotations render a secret into the pod filesystem: vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db: database/creds/app -- the deployment yaml holds a path, not a credential.
AWS CDK resolves at deploy time with secretsmanager.Secret.fromSecretNameV2, and the synthesised template carries a dynamic reference rather than the plaintext.
Terraform prefers data.aws_ssm_parameter.db_password.value over a hardcoded string so the value lives in Parameter Store and only its ARN appears in the plan.
A docker-compose.yml for local development reads env_file: .env and declares secrets: - db_password, keeping the committed manifest free of credentials.
Kustomize secretGenerator builds a Secret from a literal file at build time; the kustomization.yaml references the file and the generated Secret is applied separately.
Azure Key Vault CSI driver mounts secrets as files: the SecretProviderClass names objects and the pod reads them from /mnt/secrets-store, so no value is templated into the Deployment.
GitLab CI masks variables and injects them at job start: variables: DEPLOY_TOKEN: $DEPLOY_TOKEN, with the value held in the project's CI/CD settings.
A serverless function config uses environment: STRIPE_KEY: ${env:STRIPE_KEY} so the key comes from the deploying shell rather than the repository.
esbuild's npm package runs a postinstall that downloads the matching platform binary, which is why installing it on a new architecture fetches a different artifact.
Prisma's postinstall generates the client from schema.prisma, invoking its own engine binaries as part of a normal npm install.
